source.title: Democratizing Diplomacy: A Harness for Evaluating Any Large Language Model on Full-Press Diplomacy
source.authors: Alexander Duffy; Samuel J. Paech; Ishana Shastri; Elizabeth Karpinski; Baptiste Alloui-Cros; Tyler Marques; Matthew Lyle Olson

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper evaluates downstream strategic-game performance across models and reports a model-size trend, but it does not measure pretraining loss or reproduce a language-model loss-scaling experiment.
record.gate_note: The paper reports Diplomacy game scores, a qualitative trend toward higher scores for larger models, and a correlation with Chatbot Arena Elo. Those are downstream task outcomes, not measurements of held-out cross-entropy, parameter/token/compute power laws, extrapolation from small runs, or compute-optimal allocations. The Arena correlation is recorded as a related finding outside the claim versions because Arena Elo is not scale or pretraining loss.
record.test_reason: Weak T3 test of V6 in a new setting (full-press Diplomacy). The paper reports that larger models reach higher game scores. The evidence is a qualitative comparison across uncontrolled model families, most of undisclosed size. There is no fitted scale relation and no pretraining loss.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that larger models perform best but smaller (24B) models still play adequately, and that scores correlate with Chatbot Arena Elo (r=0.651). They also claim strategic reasoning scales with model capacity, citing Kaplan et al., with smaller gaps than on NLP benchmarks, suggesting saturation.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates strategic game performance rather than held-out language-model loss or scaling-law fits.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors state that benchmark discrimination may increase with a higher maximum game year or more trials; these alternatives are not reported as tested results here.

fits_no_version.finding: Diplomacy game score correlates with Chatbot Arena Elo (Pearson r=+0.651, Table 2, 12 models).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Performance on this Diplomacy benchmark tracks general model capability as measured by Chatbot Arena Elo.

record.peer_reviewed: AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence (venue stated in metadata); paper text says under review.
record.problems: The model-size trend is reported qualitatively, with overlapping confidence intervals; the paper does not provide a controlled parameter-count sweep or any pretraining-loss measurements.
record.rows_left_out: The reported Pearson correlation and model-specific entries in Table 2 concern Chatbot Arena Elo and Diplomacy scores, not scale or pretraining loss; the correlation is summarized as R2 under fits_no_version rather than treated as a V6 scale result.

untested.parts: All: no pretraining loss vs parameters, tokens or compute.
All: no extrapolation from small fitted runs.
All: no shape comparison at fixed parameters.
All: no power-law fits in other modalities or regimes.
Predictability from pretraining loss; any fitted or quantitative scale-to-performance relation; controlled size sweeps within one model family.
All: no exponent or fitting-choice comparison.

missing.what: Per-model Diplomacy scores. For open models of known size, these allow a direct size comparison: Llama-3.3-70B 38.1, Qwen3-235B-A22B 35.4, Mistral-Small-3.2-24B 31.1, gemma-3-12b 29.4, qwen3-30b-a3b 31.6. The ordering is non-monotone in total parameters.
Authors' statement that performance differences across sizes are smaller than on traditional NLP benchmarks, suggesting saturation at lower scales.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's fits_no_version pointed to a nonexistent row R2; I replaced it with an empty row list. The scale evidence is very weak: closed models have undisclosed sizes, and MoE total vs active parameters is ignored. The paper's main contributions are the harness, prompting, persuasion and behaviour studies, which are unrelated to scaling laws. A reviewer could reasonably classify this study as 'discusses' instead.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of larger-run pretraining loss from power laws fitted on smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its trend with compute.
Architecture comparisons at fixed parameter count.
Power-law loss behavior in other modalities or training regimes.

The study tests downstream performance in Diplomacy, not downstream performance predicted from pretraining loss; the reported model-size evidence is qualitative rather than a fitted scale relationship.
Dependence of loss-law exponents or compute-optimal allocations on fitting choices and setup.

rows.subject: evaluated models (aggregate comparison)
rows.size_stated: Different scales; the smallest models are described as 24B, but individual parameter counts are not stated here.
rows.operation_detail: Benchmark models playing France in full-press Diplomacy.
rows.measure: Diplomacy game score by model size
rows.value: Larger models progress to a higher game score on average; the smallest 24B models score the lowest.
rows.note: The text describes the direction of the trend but does not give individual scores or numerical model sizes in this passage.
rows.check: The subject and value are acceptable, but the evidence is weaker than the row implies. Size is not controlled and most models are closed with no stated parameter count. The size buckets are loose: Kimi-K2 is listed as 'medium' and Llama-3.3-70B as 'small'. Confidence intervals overlap. Table 2 shows the order is not monotone in size: Llama-3.3-70B scores 38.1 vs Qwen3-235B-A22B at 35.4. Baseline is not applicable.

relationships.condition: Off-the-shelf chat/reasoning models playing France vs six Devstral-Small opponents, 20 games to 1925, baseline prompts
relationships.reason: R1: larger models score higher on average, but CIs overlap and the order is not monotone in size. Authors say the gaps are smaller than on NLP benchmarks and suggest saturation at lower scales. Size itself is uncontrolled.
relationships.display_finding: Average scores favored larger models, but confidence intervals overlapped and rankings were nonmonotonic, with smaller gaps than on NLP benchmarks.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.reason: The reported average trend favors larger models, but confidence intervals overlap and the study does not fit or quantify a scale-to-performance relationship; see R1.
